lessons.title: Measuring and Mixing Lye Solution
lessons.body:
Lye, also called sodium hydroxide (NaOH), is the chemical that turns oils into soap. You must handle it with respect. Always wear rubber gloves, safety goggles, and a long-sleeved shirt. Work in a well-ventilated areaâideally outdoors or near an open window. Never use aluminium containers; lye reacts with aluminium and produces dangerous hydrogen gas. Use heat-resistant glass, stainless steel, or heavy plastic (PP #5).

First, weigh your lye and water separately using a digital kitchen scale accurate to 1 gram. A typical recipe for a 1 kg batch of soap might call for 130 g lye and 300 g water. Always add lye to water, never water to lye. Pouring water onto lye can cause a violent boil-up and splatter. Stir gently with a stainless steel spoon until the lye is fully dissolved. The mixture will get very hotâup to 80Â°C or more. Set it aside to cool to about 40-45Â°C before mixing with oils. You can speed cooling by placing the container in a basin of cold water.

In Africa, water quality varies. Use distilled or rain water if possible. Tap water may contain minerals that interfere with soap. If you only have tap water, boil it and let it cool to reduce some impurities. Measure carefully: too little lye leaves unsaponified oil (soft, greasy soap), too much lye makes harsh, lye-heavy soap that can burn skin. Follow your recipe exactly.

Always keep a bottle of white vinegar nearby. If lye splashes on your skin, flush with plenty of cool water, then wash with vinegar to neutralise. Never store lye solution in a closed container while hotâpressure can build up. Label your containers clearly. Keep children and animals away. After use, clean all tools with vinegar first, then soap and water.

lessons.title: Preparing and Heating Oils
lessons.body:
Cold process soap uses a blend of solid and liquid oils. Common solid oils in Africa include palm oil, coconut oil, shea butter, and cocoa butter. Liquid oils include olive oil, sunflower oil, and groundnut oil. A simple beginner recipe: 500 g palm oil, 300 g coconut oil, 200 g olive oil. Weigh each oil accurately on your scale. If you use shea butter, it often comes in chunksâgrate or chop it finely so it melts evenly.

Put all oils into a stainless steel pot. Heat gently on a low stove or charcoal stove, stirring until everything is melted. Do not overheat. Once melted, remove from heat and let it cool to about 40-45Â°C. If you don't have a thermometer, test by touch: the pot should feel warm but not hotâlike bathwater. If it's too hot, let it sit. If it's too cold, the solid oils will start to harden. You want a clear, liquid oil mixture.

In many African markets, palm oil is red and unrefined. That's fine for soapâit adds a nice orange colour and gentle cleansing. Coconut oil makes big bubbles but can be drying if used above 30% of total oils. Shea butter adds creamy lather and skin-conditioning properties. If you cannot find one oil, substitute with another from the same category (solid for solid, liquid for liquid), but keep the total weight the same. Adjusting the recipe changes the soap's qualities.

Before mixing with lye, ensure your oils are at the right temperature. If oils are too hot, they can accelerate trace and cause discoloration. If too cold, they may solidify when lye is added. Use a thermometer if you have one; if not, aim for the same warmth as your lye solution. Both should feel comfortably warm to the touch. Now you are ready to combine.

lessons.title: Achieving Emulsion and Trace
lessons.body:
Emulsion is when oil and lye water mix into a stable, creamy blend. Trace is when the mixture thickens enough that a drizzle leaves a visible trail on the surface. To get there, pour your lye solution slowly into the oils while stirring gently with a stainless steel spoon or whisk. Stir for 2-3 minutes by handâthis is called 'cooking' the mixture. You'll see it change from oily and separate to a uniform, opaque liquid. That's emulsion.

Now use an immersion blender (stick blender) to speed up trace. Pulse it in short burstsâ5 seconds on, 5 seconds offâwhile stirring by hand between pulses. Keep the blender head fully submerged to avoid splashing and introducing air bubbles. After 1-2 minutes, you'll notice the mixture thickening. To test for trace, lift your spoon and let some batter drip back into the pot. If the drip leaves a faint line that stays visible for a second or two, you have a light trace. If the line is clear and holds, that's medium trace. For most recipes, you want light to medium trace before pouring.

In hot African climates, trace can happen very fast. If your mixture becomes too thick (like pudding), you've reached heavy trace. You can still pour, but you must work quickly. To slow trace, use cooler temperatures (around 35-40Â°C) and avoid over-blending. Some essential oils, like clove or cinnamon, also accelerate trace. If you want to add colour or fragrance, do it at light trace and stir gently by handânot with the blender.

If your mixture separates after blending, don't panic. Keep blending in short bursts until it comes together. If it stays separated, your temperatures may be too far apart. Warm the oils slightly and try again. Once you have a stable emulsion and trace, you're ready to pour into molds.

lessons.title: Pouring into Molds
lessons.body:
Choose your mold based on what you have. Silicone molds are easiestâsoap pops out cleanly. Wooden molds lined with baking paper work well. Plastic containers (like ice cream tubs) can be used but may need flexible liners. Avoid metal molds unless they are stainless steel; other metals react with lye. For a 1 kg batch, a mold about 20 cm x 10 cm x 7 cm is a good size.

Pour the soap batter slowly and steadily from a low height to reduce air bubbles. If you want a swirl design, pour a small amount of coloured batter, then alternate with plain batter. Use a spoon or skewer to swirl gentlyâdon't overmix. For plain soap, just pour it all in. Tap the mold gently on the counter a few times to release trapped air. Smooth the top with a spatula or spoon.

In Africa, many soap makers use wooden boxes lined with banana leaves or plastic bags. Banana leaves give a natural look but can leave creases. Plastic bags are cheap and effectiveâjust make sure they are clean and free of holes. If you use a cardboard box, line it with baking paper or a plastic bag to prevent sticking. The mold should be deep enough to hold the batter; leave about 1 cm of space at the top for expansion during gel phase.

After pouring, cover the mold with a lid or plastic wrap. This helps keep heat in for gel phase (next lesson). If you are not insulating, you can leave it uncovered, but the soap may not gel fully. Place the mold in a safe, level spot where it won't be disturbed. Do not move it for at least 24 hours. Clean your tools immediatelyâsoap batter hardens quickly. Scrape excess batter into a separate container; you can use it to make small test bars. Now your soap needs to rest and saponify.

lessons.title: Insulating and Gel Phase
lessons.body:
Gel phase is when the soap heats up and becomes translucent, like jelly. It happens because saponification generates heat. A full gel phase makes soap harder, shinier, and more uniform in colour. Some soap makers prefer no gel for a creamier look, but for beginners, gelling is easier and faster. To encourage gel, insulate your mold. Wrap it in a thick towel or blanket, or place it in a cardboard box with a lid. In cold weather, you can add a hot water bottle next to the moldânot directly on top.

In hot African climates, gel phase can happen quickly and may even overheat. If the soap gets too hot, it can crack or develop a cavern (a hollow pocket). To prevent overheating, check your soap after 1 hour. If the mold feels very hot to the touch, remove some insulation. You can also place the mold on a wire rack to allow air circulation. A mild gel is fine; a runaway gel is not. If you see cracks, don't worryâthey can be trimmed later.

The gel phase usually lasts 1-2 hours. You'll notice the centre of the soap becomes darker and more translucent, spreading outward. Once the whole loaf looks uniform, the gel is complete. Then let it cool slowly. Do not unmold while it's still warmâit will be soft and sticky. Leave it insulated for 24 hours, then unwrap and check. If the soap is still warm, wait another 12 hours.

In very hot weather, you might skip insulation entirely. Just cover the mold with a light cloth. The soap will still saponify, but may not gel. That's okayâit will just take longer to harden. The key is to avoid drastic temperature changes. A steady, warm environment (25-30Â°C) is ideal. After 24-48 hours, your soap should be firm enough to unmold. If it's still soft, wait another day. Patience here prevents ruined batches.

lessons.title: Unmolding and Cutting
lessons.body:
After 24-48 hours, your soap should be firm enough to unmold. Test by pressing gently with your fingerâif it leaves no indent, it's ready. If it's still soft, wait another 12-24 hours. To unmold, turn the mold upside down and press on the bottom. For silicone molds, peel the sides away first. For wooden or plastic molds, you may need to tap firmly. If the soap sticks, place the mold in the freezer for 30 minutesâthe soap will shrink slightly and release. Never use a knife to pry it out; you'll damage the mold and the soap.

Once unmolded, you'll see your loaf. If you used a liner, peel it off. If the soap has rough edges or cracks, you can trim them with a knife. Now cut the loaf into bars. A standard bar is about 2.5 cm thick and 7-8 cm wide. Use a sharp, straight knife or a soap cutter. For even bars, mark the loaf with a ruler first. Cut with a gentle sawing motionâdon't press too hard, or the soap may crack. A wire cutter (like a cheese slicer) works well if you have one.

In Africa, many soap makers use a machete or a long kitchen knife. That's fineâjust keep it clean and sharp. Cut on a clean surface, like a plastic cutting board. Wear gloves if the soap is still slightly soft, as it may contain active lye. After cutting, place the bars in a single layer on a drying rack or cardboard. They need to cure for 4-6 weeks in a cool, dry, well-ventilated place. Turn them once a week so they dry evenly. Curing makes the soap milder and harder.

If you want to sell, stamp or label your bars after curing. Store them in a dry place away from direct sunlight. Properly cured soap lasts for years. Remember: the soap is still caustic when first unmoldedâwash your hands after handling. After curing, it's safe to use. Congratulationsâyou've made cold process soap from scratch!

quiz.q: What is the correct way to mix lye and water?
options: C) Mix both at the same time
D) Add lye to oil first
quiz.explanation: Always add lye to water to prevent violent boiling and splattering.

quiz.q: Which container is safe for mixing lye solution?
quiz.explanation: Stainless steel is non-reactive with lye, unlike aluminium or copper.

quiz.q: What should you keep nearby in case of lye spills on skin?
quiz.explanation: Vinegar neutralises lye and can be used to rinse affected skin after flushing with water.

quiz.q: What temperature should the lye solution and oils be before mixing?
quiz.explanation: Both should be around 40-45Â°C for proper emulsion and trace.

quiz.q: Which oil is solid at room temperature and commonly used in African soap making?
quiz.explanation: Palm oil is semi-solid in cooler climates and widely available in Africa.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of an immersion blender in cold process soap making?
quiz.explanation: An immersion blender accelerates emulsification and trace formation.

quiz.q: What does 'trace' refer to in soap making?
options: A) The colour of the soap
B) The temperature of the mixture
C) The thickness where a drizzle leaves a visible line
D) The amount of lye used
quiz.explanation: Trace is when the soap batter thickens enough to show a trail when drizzled.

quiz.q: How can you slow down trace in a hot climate?
quiz.explanation: Cooler temperatures (35-40Â°C) slow down saponification and trace.

quiz.q: Which mold material is easiest for beginners?
quiz.explanation: Silicone molds are flexible and allow soap to pop out easily without sticking.

quiz.q: Why should you tap the mold after pouring soap batter?
quiz.explanation: Tapping helps trapped air bubbles rise to the surface.

quiz.q: What is gel phase in cold process soap making?
options: A) When soap turns to liquid
B) When soap heats up and becomes translucent
quiz.explanation: Gel phase is the heating stage where soap becomes translucent and uniform.

quiz.q: How do you encourage gel phase?
quiz.explanation: Insulation traps heat generated by saponification, promoting gel.

quiz.q: What can happen if soap gets too hot during gel phase?
options: B) It cracks or forms a cavern
quiz.explanation: Overheating can cause cracks or hollow pockets in the soap loaf.

quiz.q: How long should you typically wait before unmolding soap?
quiz.explanation: Soap needs 24-48 hours to harden enough to unmold without damage.

quiz.q: What is a safe way to release stuck soap from a mold?
options: A) Use a knife to pry it
B) Place in freezer for 30 minutes
C) Pour hot water on it
D) Hit it with a hammer
quiz.explanation: Freezing shrinks the soap slightly, making it easier to release.

quiz.q: What is a standard thickness for a soap bar?
quiz.explanation: A typical bar is about 2.5 cm thick for easy handling and curing.

quiz.q: How long should cold process soap cure before use?
quiz.explanation: Curing for 4-6 weeks allows excess water to evaporate and soap to harden and milden.

quiz.q: Why should you wear gloves when handling freshly unmolded soap?
options: B) Because it may still contain active lye
quiz.explanation: Fresh soap can be caustic until fully cured; gloves protect your skin.

quiz.q: What is the recommended water type for making lye solution?
quiz.explanation: Distilled or rain water lacks minerals that can interfere with saponification.

quiz.q: What happens if you use too little lye in a recipe?
options: B) Soap becomes soft and greasy
quiz.explanation: Insufficient lye leaves unsaponified oil, resulting in soft, greasy soap.

quiz.q: Which of these oils is liquid at room temperature and commonly used in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Groundnut oil is a liquid oil widely available in African markets.

quiz.q: What is the first sign of emulsion when mixing lye and oils?
options: B) The mixture becomes uniform and opaque
quiz.explanation: Emulsion is a stable, uniform, opaque blend of oil and lye water.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid over-blending with an immersion blender?
options: A) It makes soap too hard
B) It can cause heavy trace too quickly
C) It adds too much air
quiz.explanation: Over-blending accelerates trace, making it difficult to pour or swirl.

quiz.q: What can you use to line a wooden mold if you don't have baking paper?
quiz.explanation: Banana leaves are a common natural liner in Africa and prevent sticking.

quiz.q: What is the ideal ambient temperature for curing soap?
quiz.explanation: A cool, dry, well-ventilated place around 25-30Â°C is ideal for curing.

quiz.q: How often should you turn soap bars during curing?
quiz.explanation: Turning weekly ensures even drying and prevents warping.

quiz.q: What should you do if your soap batter separates after blending?
options: C) Keep blending in short bursts
quiz.explanation: Continued short bursts of blending can bring the mixture back to emulsion.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a sign of trace?
options: A) A drizzle leaves a visible line
D) The mixture looks like pudding
quiz.explanation: Trace makes the mixture opaque and thick, not clear.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of curing soap?
options: A) To make it smell better
B) To harden it and make it milder
quiz.explanation: Curing evaporates excess water and completes saponification, making soap harder and gentler.

quiz.q: Why is it important to label containers used for lye solution?
options: B) To avoid accidental ingestion or misuse
quiz.explanation: Clear labelling prevents dangerous mistakes with a caustic substance.
